extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of social/crowd psychology
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and describe the characteristic psychological features, mechanisms, and moral tendencies of crowds (how crowds think, feel, and act) as presented in a classical social-psychology treatise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconscious phenomena predominate
rubrics_metrics.description: Unconscious phenomena play an altogether preponderating part not only in organic life, but also in the operations of the intelligence; the conscious life of the mind is of small importance in comparison with its unconscious life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most conscious acts are outcomes of an unconscious substratum shaped mainly by heredity; hidden and secret causes determine behavior far more than conscious motives. This underpins the explanation of crowd behavior: the unconscious qualities common to a race become dominant when individuals form crowds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowds weaken individual intellect and individuality
rubrics_metrics.description: In the collective mind the intellectual aptitudes of the individuals, and in consequence their individuality, are weakened; the heterogeneous is swamped by the homogeneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When individuals join a crowd their distinct intellectual capacities are diminished; crowds therefore cannot accomplish acts demanding a high degree of intelligence and tend to accumulate mediocrity rather than excellence (example: assemblies of specialists no better collectively than imbeciles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowds exhibit common, racial, and unconscious qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds possess in common ordinary qualities (the genius of a race) which are unconscious and handed down from generation to generation; these qualities become common property in crowds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General qualities of character governed by unconscious forces are shared among members of a race and become dominant in crowds; conscious elements (education, exceptional heredity) vary between individuals but are suppressed in crowds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity and loss of responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A crowd being anonymous, and in consequence irresponsible, the sentiment of responsibility which always controls individuals disappears entirely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerical anonymity gives individuals a sense of invincible power and reduces self-restraint; this facilitates yields to instincts and actions that individuals alone would restrain (explains looting, violence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical strength creates a sentiment of invincible power
rubrics_metrics.description: The individual forming part of a crowd acquires, solely from numerical considerations, a sentiment of invincible power which allows him to yield to instincts which, had he been alone, he would perforce have kept under restraint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The perception of strength in numbers removes the notion of impossibility and increases readiness to attempt acts (e.g., setting fire to a palace or pillaging) that would be restrained when alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contagion (emotional/motivational contagion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contagion is a phenomenon of which it is easy to establish the presence... In a crowd every sentiment and act is contagious, and contagious to such a degree that an individual readily sacrifices his personal interest to the collective interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contagion is classed among hypnotic phenomena; a suggestion originating in one individual spreads rapidly to others and strengthens by reciprocity, making collective action more impetuous than individual hypnotic suggestion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestibility and hypnotic-like state
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual immerged for some length of time in a crowd in action soon finds himself... in a special state which much resembles the state of fascination in which the hypnotised individual finds himself in the hands of the hypnotiser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The crowd-parthood produces a loss of conscious personality: will and discernment are lost, certain faculties are destroyed while others are exalted, and individuals obey suggestions that transform ideas into acts with irresistible impetuosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disappearance of conscious personality; predominance of unconscious
rubrics_metrics.description: The disappearance of the conscious personality, the predominance of the unconscious personality, the turning by means of suggestion and contagion of feelings and ideas in an identical direction, the tendency to immediately transform the suggested ideas into acts are principal characteristics of the individual forming part of a crowd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals become automata guided by unconscious impulses; only a few strong personalities can attempt alternative suggestions, and even then are usually overwhelmed (occasionally a felicitous expression or image can redirect a crowd).

rubrics_metrics.name: Descent on civilisational ladder (primitive/instinctive behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: By the mere fact that he forms part of an organised crowd, a man descends several rungs in the ladder of civilisation... In a crowd, he is a barbarian—that is, a creature acting by instinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even cultivated individuals act with the spontaneity, violence, ferocity, enthusiasm, and heroism of primitive beings when in crowds, and become easily impressed by words and images that would not move them individually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowds are intellectually inferior but emotionally ambivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: The crowd is always intellectually inferior to the isolated individual, but, from the point of view of feelings and of the acts these feelings provoke, the crowd may, according to circumstances, be better or worse than the individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowds' moral quality depends entirely on the nature of the suggestion to which they are exposed; they can be criminal or heroic (examples: Crusades, revolutionary/defensive actions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Impulsiveness, mobility, and irritability
rubrics_metrics.description: The crowd is at the mercy of all exterior exciting causes, and reflects their incessant variations... The impulses which the crowd obeys are so imperious as to annihilate the feeling of personal interest—Premeditation is absent from crowds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowds are slave to present stimuli, changing rapidly from ferocity to generosity; they lack long-term will or capacity for premeditation, making them very mobile and difficult to govern (examples: sudden revolutions and rapid political changes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of premeditation and short-lived enthusiasms
rubrics_metrics.description: Any display of premeditation by crowds is in consequence out of the question... Crowds are as incapable of willing as of thinking for any length of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowds act on the exciting cause of the moment; their wishes are frenzied but not durable, and democratic stability relies on everyday necessities moderating crowd impulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credulity and readiness to accept suggestion as reality
rubrics_metrics.description: In consequence, a crowd perpetually hovering on the borderland of unconsciousness, readily yielding to all suggestions... cannot be otherwise than excessively credulous. The improbable does not exist for a crowd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowds accept evoked images as real and are prone to create and propagate improbable legends and collective hallucinations (examples: Belle Poule sighting, collective misidentifications of corpses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective hallucinations and unreliability of mass testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: The mechanism of the collective hallucination... is that a suggestion made by one individual implants itself by contagion in all assembled; collective observations are as erroneous as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous eyewitnesses may agree on an erroneous account; unanimity of witnesses is often one of the worst proofs of fact. Experiments and historical examples (Mr. Davey's trick, battle eyewitness contradictions) illustrate this unreliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of the educated and ignorant in a crowd
rubrics_metrics.description: The mental quality of the individuals composing a crowd is without importance. From the moment that they form part of a crowd the learned man and the ignoramus are equally incapable of observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expertise and critical faculties vanish in matters outside one's specialty when part of a crowd; distinguished observers can be deceived (Davey's experiment), so intellectual status does not protect against crowd illusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perverse transformation and exaggeration of events by crowd imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: A crowd thinks in images, and the image itself immediately calls up a series of other images, having no logical connection with the first... The simplest event that comes under the observation of a crowd is soon totally transformed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowds conflate subjective images with objective reality, producing uniform perversions through contagion; legends and historical accounts are unstable and continually transformed by popular imagination (Napoleon legend example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration and ingenuousness of sentiments; extremes and lack of doubt
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the feelings exhibited by a crowd be good or bad, they present the double character of being very simple and very exaggerated... a throng knows neither doubt nor uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowds go straight to extremes, do not entertain nuance or doubt, and any initial antipathy rapidly escalates to furious hatred; the force of feeling is reinforced by contagious approval and absence of responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intolerance, dictatorialness, and conservatism of crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: The intolerance, dictatorialness, and conservatism of crowds... The servility of crowds in the face of a strong authority... Crowds instinctively hostile to changes and progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although momentarily revolutionary instincts may appear, crowds are often extremely conservative and hostile to change; they show servility to strong authorities and intolerance toward dissent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morality of crowds is suggestion-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: The morality of crowds, according to the suggestions under which they act, may be much lower or much higher than that of the individuals composing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowds are rarely guided by personal interest; moral outcomes depend on prevailing suggestions and can produce both higher moral action (heroism) and lower morality (criminality). Crowds can moralise and moralise poorly.
